articles.title_zh: UK police arrest dual UK-Iranian man in Fairford air base investigation
articles.content_orig:
U.K police said Thursday they arrested another man in connection with the case.
The United States knew Iran or its proxies were going to "try and do an attack, possibly on a United States asset in the [United Kingdom]," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said Thursday of the arrest and release of five men near a Royal Air Force base used by the U.S.
Mullin told Fox News the U.S. "had already been watching" the situation with British officials and the U.S. was "giving them a heads up."
His comments come after U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday he believes Iran "played a part" in last weekend's incident at a Royal Air Force base in England that hosts U.S. warplanes involved in the conflict with Iran.
"They were also feeding information to us, so this was something we were paying attention to already, we just didn't know where it was coming from" Mullin said, adding that Iran is always a threat to the United States and its allies.
"This was a little bit more specific, so we were on heightened alert about the direct threat we had here but didn't know where it was coming from, so when we saw it we were able to act quick," Mullin said.
Five British nationals from London between the ages of 23 and 25 were arrested early Sunday in possession of three vans near RAF Fairford, police said, which has long been a key hub for U.S. Air Force operations in the Middle East -- including in the conflict with Iran.
Police said the men were suspected of terrorism and explosives offenses, prompting speculation that the detainees were planning to target the RAF base, possibly on behalf of a foreign power.
Investigators said a search of the suspects' vehicles found no improvised explosive devices and authorities said they were released on bail on Monday after "extensive interviews."
On Thursday, the U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing unit announced it had arrested another man -- a dual U.K./Iranian citizen -- in connection with the case on suspicion of "preparation of terrorist acts." It also said a second man had been questioned "under caution" and that it had searched two properties.
Mullin expressed frustration that the five men were released, but "It doesn't mean these individuals are just running loose. We -- as in our partners and us -- have eyes on these five individuals. We not going to let them slip through the cracks."
Asked if he planned any response to the possible attack, President Donald Trump said Wednesday the U.S. is "studying it right now. We're studying it. We're studying it very hard."
Asked about how the U.K. has responded, Trump said, "The U.K. did release a number of people that we caught wanting to blow up a base. We caught them early and I'm trying to figure out if that's for real, if they actually did it."
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that his government believed Iran "played a part" in the possible plot.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," Burnham said.
Reacting to those accusations, Iranian Foreign Minister Aragachi said, "I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You're barking up the wrong tree."

Two years after a woman alleged a gang rape at Cornell University, renewed attention to the case and the limited consequences faced by the alleged perpetrators has raised questions about what higher education owes students who experience sexual assault on campus as well as how consent and intoxication are understood under New York law.
A woman identified as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging that she was sexually assaulted, gang-raped, and pressured to take drugs and drink alcohol by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of Oct. 19, 2024. The lawsuit is filed against the fraternity, Doe’s sorority chapter, and Cornell University; it names Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, and Scott Kretzschmar as defendants. Prosecutors said this week they were reopening a criminal investigation into the case after declining to press charges originally.
Separate attorneys for Kretzschmar and Lopes denied the allegations in statements to ABC , while Norris, via an attorney, denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use but acknowledged that he sent a message included in the complaint.
When sexual assault allegations of this kind occur on campus, they can be addressed in three distinct ways: through school disciplinary proceedings, criminal proceedings, and civil lawsuits.
Doe’s civil lawsuit alleges that Cornell failed to protect her. Her attorney has separately criticized authorities’ handling of the criminal investigation, although observers say what’s known as the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in state law could limit what prosecutors are able to charge.
Here’s what to know about how the case was handled—by Cornell and the criminal justice system—before, and what could happen next.
Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police in November 2024. According to her complaint, Cornell began its Title IX investigation on Jan. 14, 2025.
Title IX is a law dating back to 1972 that is meant to, among other things, ensure that a college investigates when there is sexual assault on campus. Central to this premise is that Title IX is meant to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
Read More: Trump’s Title IX Announcement Is Cruel. But It Does Not Change the Law
Doe’s attorney has said that Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students. Cornell has confirmed that its disciplinary process resulted in expulsions and suspensions, but has not disclosed individual outcomes. The lawsuit alleges negligence, breach of contract, and violations of New York law.
Cornell responded in a statement last week, saying that it could not confirm the individual disciplinary outcomes due to student privacy laws. However, the university clarified on Monday that “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.”
“We take sexual violence extremely seriously,” the Sept. 21 statement said. “The Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault was launched shortly after this incident and issued a REPORT in March 2026.”
In a statement Monday, Kyle Kimball, Cornell’s vice president for university relations, said Chi Phi’s Cornell chapter closed in 2024 and the fraternity remains barred from campus.
But women’s rights advocates believe that the school might not have fulfilled its legal obligations in investigating the incident and taking appropriate actions toward those involved.
Title IX is a federal civil rights law meant to prohibit sex-based discrimination in any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.
Since Title IX was introduced, courts have found that the law requires institutions to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
“The reason why Title IX addresses sexual harassment, including sexual assault, is because of the very real impact that has on students’ ability to access education,” Shiwali Patel, a Title IX expert with the National Women’s Law Center, tells TIME.
According to the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), students who experience sexual assault are more likely to earn lower GPAs in school and are more likely to drop out of school altogether.
Patel points to Doe’s attorney’s account of her efforts to leave Cornell after the alleged assault. In a Sept. 28 interview with CNN, Thomas Giuffra—Jane Doe’s lawyer—said Cornell refused her family’s tuition-refund request, leaving her to spend another semester on campus.
“She was trying to leave the institution; she didn’t want to be there,” Patel says.

House Democrats say officials may have illegally misused public funds to pay for president’s ‘narcissistic ego trips’
The Trump administration is facing growing questions over whether it illegally used taxpayer money to air television ads promoting Donald Trump five weeks before the US midterm elections .
Two congressional Democrats , Jamie Raskin of Maryland and George Whitesides of California, have asked federal watchdogs to investigate the ads.
Raskin, the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives, and Whitesides wrote to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC) on Wednesday, describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”.
The first ad was initially broadcast on 23 September. It shows dozens of images of Trump as a singer repeats “love me”, and the UFC president, Dana White, praises the president. A second ad, which aired days later, pairs footage of Trump with audio from a rally criticizing the “deep state”. Both end with fine print saying they were paid for by the US government.
“President Trump is obviously desperate for the American people to ‘love’ him, a problem that goes beyond your jurisdiction,” Raskin and Whitesides wrote in their letter. “But stealing taxpayer dollars to pay for Mr Trump’s narcissistic ego trips is plainly illegal.”
The lawmakers asked the GAO to identify the source and total amount of money used, and to issue a legal decision on whether the ads broke the law. They asked the OSC to investigate and determine who should be held accountable.
The lawmakers say the ads may violate four sets of laws , and cited a provision in this year’s spending act that bars funds for “publicity or propaganda”, along with the Anti-Deficiency Act, federal criminal statutes on misusing public money and the Hatch Act. The Hatch Act exempts the president but covers executive branch staff, and the lawmakers argue that employees must have helped produce the ads.
Raskin and Whitesides reject the White House’s description of the ads as public service announcements. They say nearly every claim in them is false, and that they are virtually identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ads. In one example, they say an ad credits Trump with reviving manufacturing, though the US has lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs in his second term, according to a February report from Congress’s joint economic committee.
They also challenge the White House’s argument that the ads are not political because Trump is not on the ballot, though at an August rally he urged supporters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot”.
A White House spokesperson has called the ads “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. Trump said on Wednesday that he would “gladly pay the money” if the ads were found to be improper.

Some Republicans have also raised concerns. The Senate majority leader, John Thune, and the senators Mike Rounds, John Kennedy and Thom Tillis have questioned the use of public money, while the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chair, Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said the ads were appropriate.
The ads are not the first administration advertising spending to draw scrutiny.
Last year the Department of Homeland Security under Kristi Noem spent more than $200m on ads promoting her and Trump’s immigration policies. In March, Noem testified that Trump had approved the campaign (which the president denied to Reuters), and he then removed her from the secretary role, relegating her to special envoy of the “Shield of the Americas”.

What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in a critical condition in hospital after Tennessee authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer says.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
A review into what happened has been ordered and executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee said.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was carried out alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17. Shipp remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law.
Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out."
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have yet to give their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike was non-fatal, although medical experts have given theories.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, told the BBC Pike probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause her breath to stop or heart failure.
The Tennessee correction department said Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility, while one of her lawyers said on Wednesday that she was being given "life-saving measures" in hospital.
On Thursday, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters: "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment."
He added: "But we do know that that she is alive right now."
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who said on Thursday that Tennessee will halt executions for the rest of the year.
This could impact any additional attempt by the state to execute Pike in the near-term, if she does regain consciousness.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".

Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years before.
A notable Supreme Court case from 1947 allowed the state of Louisiana to try a second electrocution of Willie Smith, a black teenager whose first execution attempt failed when he was 17 years old.
The court found a second execution would not violate the Constitution's prohibitions against double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment and Smith was executed aged 18.
"If the question is, is it likely the federal courts would intervene in a second attempt? I'm afraid the answer is a resounding no," Mills said of Pike's case.
Pike's lawyers have already filed a motion to stay her execution.

Maya Foa, the head of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain â lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.

"It shouldn't be a surprise something went wrong," he said.

articles.title_orig: 8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president
articles.title_zh: 8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president
articles.content_orig:
We don’t yet know how the 2026 midterm elections will shake out.
What we can say right now is that President Donald Trump’s handling of inflation is a historic liability — the likes of which we’ve rarely seen in modern American politics.
As many as 8 in 10 Americans now disapprove of Trump on that issue. That’s more than disapproved of presidents for wars gone wrong, botched crisis responses and even major scandals like Watergate.
A new AP-NORC poll on Thursday was the latest ugly data point for Trump. It showed Americans disapproved of him on cost-of-living issues by a stunning margin: 82% to 17%.
It’s rare to get even 70% of Americans to agree on anything political. But Trump has managed to unite 8 in 10 Americans against his handling of one of the country’s most important issues.
And this poll isn’t just some outlier. Here’s a brief recap of recent polls on this issue:
The level of disapproval on such a major issue has few precedents, though George W. Bush did face a 77% disapproval rating in a CBS News/New York Times poll for his handling of the economy near the end of his term after the 2008 financial crisis. In 1980, the same pollster showed Jimmy Carter’s disapproval on that issue peaking at 74% amid high unemployment and inflation.
One of the likeliest culprits for such high disapproval numbers would seem to be war. And those have been very unpopular. But not as unpopular as Trump’s handling of the cost of living. George W. Bush’s disapproval rating on the Iraq war peaked around 70% . Disapproval of Joe Biden’s withdrawal from Afghanistan peaked around two-thirds . And the Vietnam war led Lyndon Johnson to scrap his reelection bid in 1968, but his disapproval rating on the issue was only in the 60s .
In fact, the highest disapproval rating for a war appears to be Trump’s latest numbers on the Iran war. The CNN poll showed 73% disapproved of his handling of that.
When it comes to crises, as many as 64% disapproved of Bush’s handling of Hurricane Katrina, and Carter’s disapproval amid the Iran hostage crisis climbed into the mid-50s. Even Trump’s handling of the January 6 attack on the Capitol ( 67% in CNN polling ) wasn’t as lopsided as Trump and inflation right now.
As far as scandals, Ronald Reagan’s disapproval on the Iran-Contra affair reached as high as 69% in a January 1987 Washington Post-ABC News poll. And at the height of Watergate, as many as 71% of Americans disapproved of Richard Nixon on domestic issues. (We don’t have good approval polling from back then on Watergate, specifically.)
Speaking of Nixon, pardons have also tested Americans’ tolerance. But even Gerald Ford’s pardon of Nixon — which was supposed to have crippled Ford politically — only saw a disapproval rating in the 50s , according to polls compiled by the Roper Center for Public Opinion Research.
Indeed, about the closest Trump got previously to 80% disapproval on a major issue was another controversial set of pardons: his pardons of violent January 6 defendants last year. A Pew Research Center poll showed 74% of Americans disapproved of that.
You might be noticing a trend here. Many of the issues with the highest presidential disapproval ratings involve the same president: Trump. That includes the Iran war, the January 6 Capitol attack and the related pardons. But the disapproval he faces on inflation surpasses all of those issues.
You could perhaps understand why Republicans are suddenly anxious to pass legislation on affordability before the election.
Trump in a new Time magazine interview published Thursday said Americans shouldn’t hold him responsible for their affordability problems and again blamed inflation on Biden. (This despite inflation being higher today than it was when Trump took over last year.)
But the AP-NORC poll is the latest to suggest that strategy won’t work. It shows 65% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for high prices more so than factors beyond his control. That number for Biden just before the 2022 midterm elections was much lower: 44% .
Perhaps Trump’s party can still do OK in the upcoming midterms. But if it does, it will be despite historic dissatisfaction with the president on voters’ clear No. 1 issue.

Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998
Business live – latest updates
The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.
The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.
In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.
Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.
“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.
“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”
Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war , as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.
The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.
The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

articles.content_orig:
Television Business Editor
Dana Walden joked at the beginning of her Bloomberg Screentime session Thursday that her job was to “keep this seat warm for Casey Bloys, who’s bringing the real news.”
Disney’s president and chief creative officer stuck to that promise when asked about the future of Jimmy Kimmel Live! Kimmel signed a one-year contract extension in December 2025 to keep hosting the late night show through the 2026-27 season, and Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw asked Walden if the host would be sticking around.
“I’m not going to make that announcement here with you today,” Walden said. “Again, I’m letting Casey make the news.” (Bloys, the head of HBO and HBO Max, is the presumptive front-runner to head up streaming at the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery when that megamerger closes in the coming days.)
Speculation about Jimmy Kimmel Live! ‘s future has swirled since an early September Page Six story claimed Kimmel’s contract wouldn’t be renewed. ABC quickly denied that was the case, but other reports said the network is looking for significant budget cuts to keep the show going.
“The truth is, it’s a very challenging daypart,” Walden said Thursday at the Bloomberg event. “That’s not to say that Jimmy is not doing a phenomenal job, and his ratings are up. But they’re up relative to a smaller audience that’s watching late night on broadcast television.”
Kimmel and the show also have a big presence on YouTube and social media platforms, but those views and clicks bring in a fraction of the revenue that on-air advertising does. “That is not a lucrative opportunity for a very premium talk show,” said Walden.
“We’re trying to make sense of the business while also honoring a deep partnership,” she continued. “I love Jimmy; we have great friendship. He’s close to a number of the people at Disney. We’re trying to work through it and make sense of, what does Jimmy want, what’s the right thing to do, and what’s the right thing for our business.”

articles.title_orig: Judge rules Trump can’t fire court-appointed prosecutors
articles.title_zh: Judge rules Trump can’t fire court-appointed prosecutors
articles.content_orig:
Washington — A federal judge on Thursday blocked President Trump's firing of Roger Rogoff from his post as the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, finding the president cannot unilaterally remove a U.S. attorney who has been tapped to the post by a district court.
U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian delivered his decision from the bench at the end of a hearing, during which he agreed to grant Rogoff's request to reinstate him until the Senate confirms a replacement. Mr. Trump nominated Simon Peter Serrano to the position of U.S. attorney in Seattle last month.
Bastian ruled that Rogoff is the U.S. attorney in the Western District of Washington and has been the "rightful holder of that office" since July 15, when the federal district judges in the region installed him to the role and he took his oath of office.
Mr. Trump fired Rogoff less than an hour after he was sworn in.
"The real issue to be decided in this case by this court appears to be one of first impression: can the president fire a U.S. attorney appointed by the district court?" Bastian said, later adding, "The answer to the question the court is faced with is no. The president cannot unilaterally fire a United States attorney appointed by the district court."
The Justice Department said it intends to appeal and will immediately seek to halt the ruling.
In addition to declaring Rogoff as the U.S. attorney, Bastian said Charles Neil Floyd, the first assistant who has been leading the office, "is not the United States attorney" for the Western District of Washington, and authority to perform the role's responsibilities was "improperly granted."
Mr. Trump signed an order last week that directed Floyd "to perform the functions and duties of the office of United States Attorney."
"Allowing the president to fire a U.S. attorney appointed by the district court would upend the framework created by the Constitution and the statutes, which together balance the president's right to appoint and the Senate's right to confirm," Bastian said. "Allowing the president to fire a United States attorney appointed by the court also eliminates the incentive to nominate a candidate that can be confirmed by the Senate. In other words, the executive and legislative branches are supposed to and encouraged to work together."
In his oral order, the judge prohibited the Trump administration from putting Rogoff's firing into effect until the U.S. attorney spot is filled by a Senate-confirmed candidate. He also said the administration cannot purport to remove Rogoff from his position, deny him access to benefits or resources of the position, or obstruct Rogoff from his ability to carry out his duties.
Finally, Bastian said the Trump administration cannot treat anyone other than Rogoff as U.S. attorney.
"The court finds it is in the public interest that the law be followed and that Mr. Rogoff take the office to which he has already taken the oath of office," he said.
The U.S. attorney's office in Seattle has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since mid-2023. After Mr. Trump took office, he fired Tessa Gorman as the top prosecutor in the office. She had been serving temporarily before judges on the district court appointed her to the job in May 2024.
Floyd began leading the office as interim U.S. attorney in October, but his appointment was subject to a 120-day clock, which expired in February. He then began serving as first assistant U.S. attorney, the second-in-command, and said at the time that he would continue leading the office.
Because Mr. Trump had not by that time put forth a nominee to serve as the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, the district judges exercised their authority under a federal law governing U.S. attorney vacancies to tap Rogoff for the job. That law allows the attorney general to appoint an interim U.S. attorney, who is subject to a 120-day term. Once that appointment expires, the district court can either agree to extend that prosecutor's tenure or appoint its own U.S. attorney until the Senate confirms a replacement.
Following his swift firing, Rogoff filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration and argued that his removal was unlawful. He argued that if not blocked by the court, the Trump administration's "actions will permit the Executive Branch to evade the Senate's advice-and-consent role indefinitely."
Mr. Trump has attempted to install his preferred candidates for U.S. attorney in several other places, including Nevada, New York, Virginia and New Jersey. Federal courts have in those instances, some of which involve a slightly different mechanism, found the appointments unlawful.
Rogoff, however, appears to be the first ousted prosecutor to challenge his firing in court.

Editorial Director/Box Office Editor
Well, on the bright side of things, the autumn box office should continue at a great hum this weekend thanks to Amazon MGM Studios’ feature take on the Colleen Hoover thriller Verity , starring Dakota Johnson, Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett. The domestic outlook is $30 million-plus at 3,510 theaters, with the definite potential to overperform given how there’s walk-up business from Hoover-philes.
The Michael Showalter-directed thriller also has a shot at $20M-$25M in 70 offshore territories sans Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and CIS in this suite, which would be a $50M-$55M global start. Previews stateside start Thursday on Verity at 2 p.m.
Meanwhile, light candles and say prayers for Warner Bros/Legendary Entertainment’s Tom Cruise -starring, Alejandro G. Iñárritu-directed Digger . Many are bracing for what could be one of Cruise’s lowest wide openings at the box office of the millennium. Warners believes the movie can get to $12M-$15M at 3,300 theaters; others believe it’d lucky to break $10M at the domestic box office.
Seventy-three foreign territories except Poland, Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand (no China release) are expected to deliver another $15M-$20M abroad for Digger at 14,000+ screens, which would mean a $35M global start at the high end for the reported net $125M production (rumors suggest the movie cost much higher, between $140M-$150M).
Unlike the Dune franchise, Legendary didn’t co-finance Digger , but they did produce it. Previews start at 2 p.m. in North America, with tickets on sale in Imax, Dolby Cinema, VistaVision, PLFs and motion seats.
Digger was shot at Leavesden Studios with UK tax credits; the global marketing spend is approaching $100M. To say that the movie is divisive is an understatement, with some critics hailing the brilliance of the polemic movie and its Doctor Strangelove satire, while others were simply impatient watching it. Current Rotten Tomatoes critical score is 52%, and know that Cruise has had lower ratings (2017’s The Mummy was 15% Rotten with reviewers, and 2016’s Jack Reacher: Never Go Back was 37% Rotten). Warners in a last-minute marketing salvo is leaning into selling the controversy of the film with a final spot, this tweet having clocked 2.2 million views:
Decide for yourself. DIGGER – in theaters and IMAX FRIDAY. Tickets on sale now. https://t.co/Z1IpSpFnXd pic.twitter.com/e5ID4WUxbL
Back in his heyday as a star, Cruise posted low openings at the domestic box office in the single-digit range (i.e., the classic Rain Man opened to $7M in 1988 at 1,248 theaters and powered to $172.8M domestic), but those were different distribution days when movies opened small and played long. Post-2000, some of Cruise’s lowest North American opening have included the 2007 drama Lions for Lambs ($6.7M; $35M production cost), 2012’s Rock of Ages ($14.4M; $75M production cost), Jack Reacher ($15.2M and $60M production cost, though it spawned a Prime Video TV franchise) and 2017’s American Made ($16.7M; $60M net production).

The arguments made for his spendy Mission: Impossible movies, particularly the last two, is that they’re bound to profit in their nth cycle (You gotta look at the overall library not just the individual movie, Paramount says in defending that franchise).
What positive things are there to say about Digger at this point? Domestic tracking in first choice climbed from a 2 since landing on tracking to a 7, which is the same as Cruise’s American Made and higher than Marty Supreme ($17.7M opening). Back to Verity. We hear U.S./Canada presales are behind It Ends With Us ($50M opening; $148.5M domestic final, $351.4M WW) , but that’s not a bad thing. That movie was Hoover’s most popular novel, and it opened when Blake Lively was in the mega-ether of Deadpool & Wolverine. Not to mention female audiences were intrigued by the percolating crisis between Lively and her co-star/director Justin Baldoni (fans were already deconstructing bad blood between them from red-carpet photos alone).
Hollywood went on a buying spree, snapping up Hoover tomes for the big screen. Two of them, Paramount’s Regretting You ($13.6M opening, $48.8M domestic, $90.4M WW) and Reminders of Him ($17.9M opening, $48.5M domestic, $89.2M WW) were all right in regards to their budgets, but not box office sensations. Verity is arguably Hoover’s second-most popular novel.
Like-for-like comps for Verity abroad are above The Drama ($9.4M international opening), lit thriller Where the Crawdads Sing ($12M) and Reminders of Him ($10M, though that was in 56 territories). The lit adaptation should do well in Europe, specifically Scandinavia, and we’re hearing advance ticket sales are really hot in Brazil, where Verity is above It Ends With Us. In like-for-likes, It Ends With Us had a $45.6M opening.

Also opening stateside in 1,350 theaters this frame is Lionsgate Premiere’s horror pic Beware Boiuna from filmmaker Mike P. Nelson, which is looking at single digits. Blurb: A team of doctors embark on a local mission in the Amazon rainforest, but it soon becomes clear that not everybody — or everything — is happy to see them. Their sudden appearance draws the attention of an animal predator, the “Boiúna.”
Meanwhile, don’t count out A24’s Primetime. Many thought the pic would be front-loaded, but it has posted solid weekdays and is now up to a running total of $23.8M. The Lance Oppenheim-directed movie starring Robert Pattinson could hold to better than -60%.
Older adults will continue to go to Paramount’s Brad Pitt survival movie The Heart of the Beast, with a second-weekend dip of around 40%. Its U.S./Canada cume currently is $26M. articles.content_orig:
Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998
Business live – latest updates
The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.
The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.
In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.
Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.
“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.
“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”
Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war , as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.
The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.
The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ruled out a ceasefire on long-range strikes with Ukraine as Moscow steps up its campaign of aerial attacks on Kyiv .
“We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships.’ It is simply ridiculous,” Putin said on Thursday at the Valdai political forum in Moscow.
The remarks followed a meeting between United States President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on September 22, when Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow also stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Speaking at the forum of the Moscow-based think tank, Putin said Ukraine had “partially achieved its objectives” with ⁠these strikes, with attacks on Russian ⁠oil refineries having cost the country 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), but added that Russia ⁠was now responding in kind.
Russia has ramped up long-range strikes, targeting Ukraine’s steel companies as well as supply chains, notably in the rail sector. Ukraine accuses Moscow of deliberately hitting civilian targets and keeping Kyiv on a near-constant state of alert as it braces for another tough winter.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, according to city officials, as the Ukrainian capital endured relentless aerial attacks. No casualties were reported as children and staff at the school were in shelters when the drone hit.
Putin added that Russia would prefer to end the conflict in Ukraine through talks and wanted it to ⁠be a neutral ⁠country after the end ⁠of hostilities.
He warned the West not to escalate the standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania, and pledged to defend it with nuclear weapons if necessary.
“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well – the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda,” he said.
Putin’s comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia’s Baltic exclave.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict ⁠could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios. “We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” ⁠he said.
On the contrary, in the event of a “favourable scenario”, Putin said the assets of Western companies that Moscow had seized could potentially be returned. Putin last month ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro.

A spot in the semifinals is on the line Thursday night as the Las Vegas Aces host the Indiana Fever in a decisive Game 3 in their first-round playoff series. The reigning champion Aces took Game 1 at home on Sunday before falling on the road in Indy on Tuesday. The teams are back in Vegas on Thursday, and the Game 3 winner will move on to face either the Golden State Valkyries or Dallas Wings in the semifinals.
Caitlin Clark picked up the first playoff win of her career on Tuesday, posting 27 points and 15 rebounds as the Fever kept their season alive. A'ja Wilson had a monster Game 1 (38 points on 15-of-19 shooting and 16 rebounds), and she followed it up with a 22-point showing in the Game 2 loss. Wilson also got a technical foul after getting into an altercation with an Indiana fan on Tuesday night.
So what does Game 3 have in store? CBS Sports will have live updates and analysis throughout the night. Follow along below.
Aces forward Stephanie Talbot popped up on the injury report ahead of Game 3 with a left leg injury. She has officially been listed as questionable, and Aces coach Becky Hammon told reporters that Talbot will be a game-time decision.
It's unclear when Talbot, the Aces' starting small forward, was injured. She played 28 minutes in Game 2 and was on the floor until the Aces waved the white flag in the final minute.
While Talbot doesn't put up huge numbers, she's been playing very well since the World Cup. In this series, she has taken the Caitlin Clark matchup and given the Fever star a bit of trouble at times with her size. If Talbot cannot go, the Aces would likely move Jewell Loyd into the starting lineup, which would make them much smaller and further weaken their depth. articles.title_orig: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
articles.title_zh: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
articles.content_orig:
Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
The disgraced hip-hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs.
They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which include video of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source.
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved.
“For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said.
TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary.
Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say.
“We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s.
Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones.
“A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said.
Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or gray sweatpants and shirts.
Meals are delivered in trays, but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink.
“It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said.
It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate.
He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday.
The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.)
“These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement.
Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein .
Combs’ trial last year centered on drug-fueled orgies he organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers and his former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
The trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on the more serious charges of sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.
Chloe Melas is an entertainment correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Friendly-faced California tech CEO arrested by feds for allegedly hiding $300M Chinese secret
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Friendly-faced California tech CEO arrested by feds for allegedly hiding $300M Chinese secret
articles.content_orig:
Federal agents on Wednesday arrested a California tech CEO who’s accused of smuggling more than $300 million in restricted AI chips into China.
Greg Lui, 38, aka “Yiu Kong Lui,” of San Gabriel, faces a barrage of federal charges for allegedly selling Beijing a mountain of American-made AI graphics processors in violation of US laws, potentially threatening national security.
The California Post watched as the FBI and Department of Commerce agents arrested the high-flying tech boss in a stealth raid at the City of Industry headquarters of Earthmade Computers, a company Lui founded and runs, and which he allegedly used to conduct the profitable yet illegal scheme.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Agents tracked Lui as he drove a Tesla Cybertruck with a white wrap from his gigantic San Gabriel mansion to the Earthmade’s shiny offices in a tidy industrial park, handcuffing him at gunpoint soon after he arrived at work. Lui didn’t speak as he was placed in a vehicle to be taken in for processing.
AI is now used in nearly every aspect of modern warfare, and investigators said the advanced tech allegedly smuggled by Lui could’ve easily been put to use by the Chinese military.
“Protecting America’s national security means keeping our advanced Super Intelligence technology from being used to strengthen our adversaries’ military capabilities,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli.
“This defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than $300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China,” Essayli added. We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit.”
Federal prosecutors say Lui and his co-conspirators used Earthmade to buy and send sensitive AI tech into China from 2023 to 2024, without the required licenses issued by DOC that are meant to promote US foreign policy and protect national security.
Instead, they shipped these items to countries such as Malaysia and Singapore, where no licenses are required, and then illegally re-exported them to China.
The items in question were high-end computer servers, containing processors made by Nvidia Corp , a Santa Clara tech company specializing in AI. According to federal regulations, such tech could make significant contributions to Chinese armed forces.
As part of the alleged scheme, prosecutors say, Lui and his conspirators used fake documents to show the potentially dangerous AI tech would be going to destinations that did not require an export license in orders they placed with suppliers such as Nvidia.
After making these orders, Lui hired freight forwarding companies to ship the processors to Malaysia and Singapore . Once the servers arrived in these locations, Lui worked with his conspirators to reship the items to China.
From January 2024 to October 2024, Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies as part of the scheme, according to court papers.
Prosecutors say Lui executed the scam knowing what he did was illegal, and they have the evidence to prove it.
For example, prosecutors say, Lui emailed a conspirator in January 2024 saying a Malaysian transshipment company wanted to buy 70 computer servers with the controlled AI tech. In the email, he noted the laws against the sale of such tech, according to court papers.
Later that month Lui purchased 27 of the servers for roughly $7.6 million and sent the servers from LA to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Two months later, one of Lui’s conspirators told a Malaysian official in an email that the servers had, in fact, been transshipped to China.
Prosecutors say Lui used a LA-based JP Morgan Chase account and Bank of America account to send and receive money to orchestrate the scheme.
Lui is charged with one count of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act , one count of smuggling and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. If convicted he faces up to 50 years in prison.
Before his arrest Lui lived a luxurious lifestyle, recently completing an extensive renovation of the 4,300-square foot mansion on Walnut Grove Avenue that he used to house numerous members of his extended family.
Federal agents were seen conducting a search of the massive spread Thursday, recording video and carrying evidence from the nine-bedroom, seven-bathroom home that has two stories and just got new stucco and windows, a fresh driveway and other upgrades.
The US DOC, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service and the FBI are investigating the case.
According to his LinkedIn page, Lui has an eight-year career in tech that began with a stint at Amplitude Tech Hosting Service, a Denver-based firm specializing in database colocation.
In 2021 he founded Earthmade Computer, which also handles database colocation, in addition to computer processor procurement and export, according to LinkedIn.
Before his tech run, Lui was a restauranter who specialized in ultra-spicy Sichuan Chinese food. In 2012 he co-founded of Duo-Pot in Arcadia, a Chinese hot pot and dry pot joint that sold spicy frog dishes before it closed in 2021, according to LinkedIn.

articles.title_orig: Former Dallas officer convicted of killing Black man in his apartment granted parole
articles.title_zh: Former Dallas officer convicted of killing Black man in his apartment granted parole
articles.content_orig:
A former Dallas police officer was granted parole on Thursday just under seven years after she was convicted of murdering her neighbor in a 2018 shooting.
Amber Guyger , 38, was granted parole by the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles, the board said in a statement. In 2019, Guyger was convicted of murdering 26-year-old Black man Botham Jean.
Guyger told authorities that she shot Jean after mistakenly walking into his apartment, believing it to be her own, according to officials. She told authorities she believed Jean was an intruder. Jean was eating ice cream in his living room and not armed, according to authorities.
The former police officer was sentenced to 10 years in prison for the crime. Prosecutors asked jurors to sentence Guyger to at least 28 years.
The Texas board said that Guyger was granted parole because she did not have a documented pattern of violent arrests, she “maintained a satisfactory institutional adjustment” and completed programs “that should enhance chances to obtain and maintain full-time stable employment” during her imprisonment.
Guyger initially became eligible for parole on September 29, 2024. Her initial review occurred on October 10, 2024, and resulted in a parole denial with her next review being scheduled on or about October 2026.
During her trial, questions were raised about the role race may have played in the killing.
Prosecutors revealed racist text messages the former police officer sent, unrelated to Jean or his killing.
One of the texts was about the Martin Luther King Jr. parade in Dallas in 2018.
“When does this end lol,” an officer wrote to Guyger.
“When MLK is dead … oh wait …,” she joked.
Two days before Guyger killed Jean, she texted someone who had just adopted a German Shepherd.
The dog’s owner wrote that the dog “may be racist.”
Guyger replied: “It’s okay ... I’m the same.”
Prosecutors said that Jean was watching television and eating a bowl of vanilla ice cream in his living room just before 10 p.m. when Guyger burst inside and shot him.
Guyger testified that she used her electronic key fob to open Jean’s door and that she immediately drew her service weapon once she was inside.
The prosecution said the trajectory of the bullet showed that Jean was either getting up from his couch or cowering when Guyger fired at him.
A lawyer for Jean’s family, Lee Merritt, said in a statement to NBC News Dallas-Fort Worth that the family was “disappointed by the decision.”
“A 10-year sentence was already a fraction of what was lost,” Merritt said. “Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system. It is not. The family still lives with this loss every day.”
Jean’s family said in a statement on Thursday that they are requesting privacy at this time.
“To all of the many well-wishers who have continued to say Botham’s name and carry his memory, they wish to give their thanks for the continuing support,” the family said in a statement.
Jean’s brother, Brandt Jean, said he forgave Guyger during her sentencing in 2019.
“I personally want the best for you,” he said at the time. “I wasn’t even going to say this before my family, but I don’t even want you to go to jail. I want the best for you, because I know that’s exactly what Botham would want you to do — to give your life to Christ.”
The Dallas Police Department said in a statement that it had “no role in this decision.”
“The Dallas Police Department understands this decision may bring renewed attention and emotion surrounding the tragic death of Botham Jean,” the department said. “Our thoughts remain with the Jean family and all those impacted by his loss.”
Jean grew up in Saint Lucia before coming to the United States to go to Harding University in Arkansas, which he graduated from in 2016. He was working as an accountant for one of the most prestigious accounting firms in the world, PricewaterhouseCoopers, in Dallas when he was killed.
He would have turned 35-years-old on Tuesday.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu: Omani co-pilot went through Islamic radicalization
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu: Omani co-pilot went through Islamic radicalization
articles.content_orig:
Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens
The Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu , has claimed.
Israeli passengers intervened to stop the attack on Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane was able to stabilise the plummeting plane and ultimately land it safely in Saudi Arabia.
The plane had more than 170 people onboard and Israeli officials praised the bravery of those who intervened, announcing that four of the Israeli passengers would receive a “heroism” award for preventing a potential disaster.
Netanyahu told Fox News: “We know that he underwent Islamic radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information.”
The co-pilot, whose identity is still not known, was being interrogated by Saudi security services, which arrested him on the plane’s arrival in Tabuk, in the north-west of the country.
Saudi investigators were cooperating with the United Arab Emirates , the US, Oman and Israel to try to determine the attacker’s motive, a regional official familiar with the investigation said. “All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” they told the Associated Press.
Two Israeli security officials said that Israel’s initial assessment was that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, Reuters reported.
Netanyahu said that the co-pilot was probably suicidal, citing preliminary “indications”.
“It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue,” he said, emphasising that final conclusions had yet to be made.
Netanyahu had previously said it was “too early to say” if there was any state backing – namely Iranian – of the attack. Two Israeli security sources told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.
The attack came just days after Netanyahu warned of an unspecified security threat to Israel that could come during its October election. The Israeli military had said before the incident it had no specific intelligence of an imminent threat and the opposition leader Yair Lapid said that a security briefing on Tuesday night included no mention of a related threat.
Other Israeli officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, and the ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, suggested the incident was a “terror attack”, with the Israeli foreign ministry briefing its diplomats that the attack was against Israel and its relationship with the UAE.
Donald Trump suggested the co-pilot was “perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”, and told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu had spoken at length.
Netanyahu also spoke to the president of the UAE, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed to Israel’s involvement in the investigation.
Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation took place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.
The UAE announced on Thursday that it would conduct its own investigation into the incident, which started about two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai. It said its investigators had begun to look into the attacker’s motive and if he had any links to any “terrorist purpose”.
Passengers said they saw a knife-wielding man – apparently the Omani co-pilot – putting the captain of the plane on the floor, after which the plane began to plummet. The wounded pilot, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to send out an emergency signal and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and stop the plane’s descent.
A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed one passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events onboard had played out.
Hayoun told the prime minister he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.
Machchhar was widely praised for his bravery, with Netanyahu and the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, hailing him as a hero. India’s ambassador to the UAE met the wounded captain’s family and briefed them on his recovery, the Indian consulate in the UAE said.
Machchhar was being treated in a hospital in Tabuk , but was in good health and recovering well, according to the Indian embassy in the UAE, which said the ambassador had visited the pilot.
“Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO,” Modi said, in a post on social media. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.”

The Eagles have had the Rams' number in recent seasons, but it feels like that run is soon to be over.
For the gambling degenerates, here are my Week 4 NFL picks. The team logos indicate who I think will win the game, not cover the spread. At the end of the picks, I'll note a few teams that I like based on the spread.
Steelers (-3) at Browns : A serial sexual assaulter vs. a weirdo conspiracy theorist. Bad Thursday Night Football is back!
Shockingly, the serial sexual assaulter actually hasn't been a horrible quarterback so far this season, while the weirdo conspiracy theorist was cooked a long time ago. Give me the Browns, with no confidence whatsoever.
(I guess I'll instead be tuning into the Phils' inevitable soul-crushing season-ending loss.)
Colts (-4) vs. Commanders (in London) : Jayden Daniels had a spectacular rookie season, but has not been good since. Lately, I really don't think there's much of a dropoff from him to QB2 Marcus Mariota.
The Colts were a team that I thought could maybe sneak up on teams like they did at the start of the 2025 season, because I like their offensive line. But, Daniel Jones just kind of is who he is after a promising 2025 season, as he has accounted for 3 TDs and 5 turnovers.
This is the first 9:30 a.m. game of the season, by the way.
Rams (-3) at Eagles : The Rams are 1-2, but obviously they are a very talented football team, with an MVP quarterback and one of the best wide receiver duos in the NFL. They got waxed Week 1 in Australia, partly because of idiotic travel plans, but have played a lot better since, and frankly were robbed of a win in Denver Week 3.
Conversely, on both sides of the ball, the Eagles have looked sloppy, disorganized, and they have surprisingly been beaten in the trenches through the first three weeks of the season. The only reason they're 2-1 is because Jalen Hurts made a bunch of plays against bad teams the first two weeks. That is not a sustainable winning formula, and sure enough when they finally played a decent team, they got thoroughly outclassed, even with that team starting a quarterback who hadn't thrown a pass in a real game in three years.
During the Nick Sirianni era, we've seen the Eagles figure out ways to beat good teams, but it's hard to see that here with the way they look at the start of this season, even with Hurts playing reasonably well.
Patriots at Bills (-6.5) : Drake Maye has thrown for 1 TD vs. 6 INTs, and just looks lost. He got crowned WAY to early. Meanwhile, the Bills have looked so far like one of the best teams in the NFL.
Jets at Bears (-3.5) : Obviously this line is only 3.5 points because Caleb Williams isn't expected to play. It'd be pretty embarrassing if the Jets beat this Bears team that just destroyed the Eagles.
Cardinals (-2.5) at Giants : These teams are probably equally bad. So, I dunno, I'll take the home team, I guess. Side note: Here are the Giants' next six opponents, and their DVOA rankings:
• Week 4: Cardinals: 19th • Week 5: Commanders: 26th • Week 6: Saints: 28th • Week 7: Texans: 17th • Week 8: Eagles: 22nd • Week 9: Commanders: 26th
It's going to be funny when they're 5-4 and they're buyers at the trade deadline despite having absolutely no shot at contending this season.
Cowboys at Texans (-3) : The Texans can't run the ball, and they can't protect the quarterback. Those two things were very predictable before the season began, and yet this team was a popular Super Bowl pick for a lot of people. I don't know how anyone looked at that offensive line and thought, "Yep, Super Bowl, baby."
The Cowboys are over-hyped, too, but that's nothing new. But at least they can score points.
Jaguars at Bengals (-2.5) : The Jaguars are legitimate Super Bowl contenders. They're just really good in all three phases.
The Bengals' defense looked halfway decent for a couple games to start the season, but it is once again hard to take them seriously after they gave up 400+ yards to a bad Steelers offense.
Packers (-3.5) at Buccaneers : The Packers are frauds, but so are the Bucs, who are forced to start an undrafted rookie free agent at quarterback after Baker Mayfield dislocated his thumb last week.
Titans at Ravens (-11.5) : Pretty easy survivor pool pick here.
Dolphins at Vikings (-10.5) : Also not a bad survivor pool play.
Broncos at 49ers (-2.5) : Interesting matchup. Brock Purdy is playing really well. He's 60 of 83 (72.3%), for 789 yards (9.5 YPA), 9 TDs and 1 INT. He has also made some plays with his legs, running 10 times for 93 yards and a TD. He'd probably be my pick for MVP if the season ended today (it doesn't).
The Broncos should be 1-2.
Chiefs (-4.5) at Raiders : The Raiders are the shocking team of this young NFL season, at 3-0. And they've won their games by 14, 12, and 8, so it's not as if these wins are flukes. But... the Chiefs are also 3-0, and it's a lot easier to trust them.
Chargers at Seahawks (-7) : The Seahawks had a little bump in the road in their loss to the Commanders Week 3, but they're tough and well-coached and should bounce back. I'm not so sure Justin Herbert and the Chargers have that same bounce-back gene after their 0-3 start. They're desperate for a win, and I don't see that coming this week.
Lions (-3.5) at Panthers : I trust that the Lions can score a lot of points. I don't trust much else about either of these two teams.
Falcons at Saints (-2.5) : Oh hey the Falcons are playing a prime-time game for the second straight week. Not sure why we needed that. I do like some of their playmakers on offense, and Bijan Robinson is a superstar player. I also think the Saints are premature hipster team that has become a little overrated.
Weekly disclaimer: Technically, I was out Week 1. However, in the survivor pool I'm in you're allowed to buy back in if you get knocked out Week 1. With that in mind — and because "survivor pool" is in the headline and it would be weird for it to just not exist here all season — I'm just going to keep on going.

articles.title_zh: Following loss, Willson Contreras critical of Red Sox’ reliance on data and analytics
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK — For the Red Sox, the playoffs had barely begun by the time the Yankees delivered a sledgehammer of shattering finality.
In two games, the Sox were outscored, 18-2, in the most lopsided Wild Card Series in the brief history of the best-of-three format. Their 9-0 blanking at the hands of Cam Schlittler and the Yankees in Game 1 was followed by a 9-2 slobberknocking in Game 2 that spelled the end of the series and the season.
How to make sense of the shellacking?
“It’s a good question. It’s different for everybody,” said Trevor Story. “You work your [butt] off all year, all offseason, and you get to this point, and this is what we play for. You play to win in the postseason, and to have it end [in Yankee Stadium] two times in a row is tough, and everyone will process that differently.”
For some players, there was appreciation of the zombie-like midyear return from the dead, a 15-game winning streak and 32-5 stretch unlike anything that most of the players had experienced. Yet the traces of those summer memories were clouded by the thrashing they’d just endured.
The Sox hit .117 (7 for 60) — the second-worst average by any team in any playoff series. Their .159 on-base percentage was the lowest. They barely had any runners in scoring position in the two games, and when they did, they literally did nothing, going 0 for 3 with nary a base runner.
Willson Contreras was in little mood for silver linings. At 34, he is their elder statesperson among position players. He was the team’s best hitter this year, hitting .275/.386/.516 with career highs in on-base and home runs (27). He is an influential clubhouse voice.
Despite playing through a number of injuries, he was their one source of offense Wednesday, going 2 for 2 with a homer and a pair of walks. His four times on base doubled the combined total of the rest of the lineup.
“We didn’t play good at all,” he said. “We didn’t pitch. We didn’t hit. And when you don’t have those two it’s tough to win. [The Yankees] played better than us.”
For Contreras, that straightforward analysis was the beginning of a critique of the Red Sox organization that sharpened as he continued.
“I’m really proud of this group, [but] whatever we did in the past stays in the past,” he said. “We have to get better for next year. In every aspect of the game, we have to get better. That’s the bottom line.”
How did an offense that was tops in the American League for a 60-game stretch (5.18 runs per game from June 25 through Aug. 31) regress to early-season form by staggering through September (an MLB-worst 2.96 runs per game) and then collapse in a brief postseason?
“That’s a good question. I’m not going to answer it because I don’t want to give my honest answer,” said Contreras. “We got eliminated. That’s the bottom line … We didn’t produce. We didn’t execute any part of the game. And that’s why we [lost].
“I know we had a really good stretch. I’m really proud of what we did in the past, like I said. We were able to turn the season around for sure, 100 percent, but that’s not enough. It’s not enough.”
Contreras suggested both specific areas in which the Sox needed to improve — for instance, controlling the running game of opponents — but also macro-level adjustments.
“It’s not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers telling you what to do. This is baseball and the data is here to help us,” he said. “But at the end of the day, you’re going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff that I would love to say but I’ll stay [with] that.”
Does Contreras believe the Sox are too data-reliant?
“If you watch the game,” Contreras responded incredulously, implying that the answer was obvious. “If you watch the game.”
Given that view, is there anything Contreras or other players can do to encourage the organization to evolve in its approach?
“I don’t know. I cannot make decisions,” he said. “The only thing that I can control is my part of the game … Making decisions about data, about all that stuff, we cannot do anything about it. Like I said, it’s here to help us. But at the end of the day, it’s not about data. It’s about executing the game plan.
“At the end of the day, we can talk, we can share ideas. I’m not making decisions and we’re not going to make decisions. We are employees. We get paid to play baseball, and we play to be out there on the field, to perform. That’s the bottom line.”
Despite his misgivings, Contreras — who had to waive his no-trade protection in order to complete his December trade from the Cardinals to the Red Sox — suggested he is content in the organization.
“I really had fun,” said Contreras, whose contract has one more guaranteed year, plus a team option for 2028. “This [was] my first season in Boston. I didn’t have any expectations coming up here when I got traded. I didn’t want to put anything in my mind.
“[But] I’m really proud [with] what I was able to do during the whole season,” he said. “But also, I’m proud of the team that we’ve got here and proud of everybody.”
